title: Politics chat: The polls show a Democratic sweep in the midterms. Can you trust them?
description: If you look at the few truly competitive seats, polls show a more complicated picture of momentum toward the Democratic Party in midterm House
body:
If you look at the few truly competitive seats, polls show a more complicated picture of momentum toward the Democratic Party in midterm House races. For the Senate, Republicans are on defense.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)BARACK OBAMA: And there's gold everywhere. What's up with the gold?(LAUGHTER)AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:  That's President Obama on the campaign trail this weekend.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)OBAMA: He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.(LAUGHTER)RASCOE: The former president in Ohio there, commenting on the current president, who's not on the ballot next week but kind of is. NPR's senior national political correspondent Mara Liasson joins us now. Good morning, Mara.MARA LIASSON, BYLINE: Good morning.RASCOE: Ten days until Election Day. Many votes, of course, already cast, but that's not stopping the pollsters.LIASSON: That's right. Polls show that Donald Trump is now at his lowest approval rating ever. In the Washington Post/ABC News/Ipsos poll, 71% of voters say gas is unaffordable. That's a 43% jump from February. Trump's approval rating on the economy has fallen from 45% in February, which is pretty low, to now under 30%. And we - doesn't tell you whether voters - former Trump supporters are going to turn out and vote for Democrats, but it does show you how deep the hole Republicans are in.RASCOE: So the polls are bad for Republicans, but are they accurate? Because, you know, we've seen some shaky performances from polling firms in recent years.LIASSON: Well, we'll find out on Election Day if they're accurate, but there is something that consumers of polls should remember - that the generic congressional ballot question can be confusing. It keeps on getting bigger for Democrats. It's basically the question is - do you prefer a generic Democrat or a generic Republican to win your House seat? It's supposed to be a proxy for the national popular vote for the House. The problem is that with extreme gerrymandering, it's not that relevant anymore because there are so few actually competitive districts, districts that went for Harris or Trump by 5 points or less.So the thing that's more relevant is, what is the generic congressional ballot in just those dozen or so competitive seats? And there are some polls that measure that. And those polls show that instead of 8 or 9 or 11 points ahead, as Democrats are nationally in the generic ballot question, in those competitive seats, they're only two or three points ahead. So it tells you how close those competitive House races are, and those are the races that are going to determine how big a majority Democrats get if they win the House.RASCOE: And that's the House. How about the Senate, where every race is a statewide race?LIASSON: When you look at the races that are going to determine control of the Senate, most of them - Alaska, Texas, Ohio, Iowa - they are all toss-ups. Trump won them back in 2024 by an average of 13 points. These are very red states, and Democrats to win them have to do more than just motivate their base. Their base just isn't big enough in those states. They're going to have to flip Republican votes, and that's hard for voters in red states who voted for Republicans their whole lives. So those states are all still too close to call.RASCOE: Alaska's Senate race is really competitive. The Trump administration just filed a lawsuit about it. What's your take there?LIASSON: Well, the Trump administration is asking a federal court to block certification of the Senate election results in Alaska if the Republican incumbent narrowly loses. This has never happened before. Their argument is that there are two people on the ballot with similar names. One is the incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan, and one is another candidate running, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. The Trump administration is saying that could confuse voters and voters might mistakenly vote for the wrong Dan Sullivan. This has already gone to the Alaska state courts, which have ruled that it's fine to have both Dan Sullivans on the ballot.The Alaska Senate race is very close. The Democratic candidate Mary Peltola has been running ahead by a few points of Dan S. Sullivan, the incumbent, and election experts say it's unlikely the suit will prevail, since the Constitution gives states, not the federal government, the right to control the way elections are conducted. But the suit is saying that it wants a delay in certification until it can conduct an investigation to determine whether voters really meant to cast their votes for the Dan Sullivan that they chose. Unclear how they would do that.RASCOE: And quickly on the controversy in Ohio, where we heard from President Obama this weekend. Talk to me about that.LIASSON: Well, this is a very controversial ad gubernatorial candidate Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is running, featuring the mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, telling voters that she's a liar and they shouldn't vote for her. The backstory is that Amy Acton and her brother were removed from custody of her mother more than 50 years ago after her stepfather was indicted for raping her. And many Republicans have spoken out against this ad, including the governor of Ohio, who said it's just plain wrong. Donald Trump, however, says he thinks the ad is great. And the big question that this controversy raises is, can anyone besides Trump pull off this kind of campaigning?RASCOE: That's NPR's Mara Liasson. Mara, thank you so much.LIASSON: You're welcome.

title: Trump escalates anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed in Michigan
description: President Donald Trump departs after spe
body:
President Donald Trump departs after speaking during a campaign rally at McMorran Place Sports and Entertainment Center, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026, in Port Huron, Mich.
                
                    Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
    

   
   PORT HURON, Mich. — President Donald Trump intensified his anti-Muslim rhetoric against Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday, portraying him as a threat to national security and questioning his loyalty to the United States in remarks that drew a sharp rebuke from a former top Arab American ally.   
   Trump called El-Sayed, a former Detroit health official, a "jihadist" who was "on the side of the terrorists" and would "have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go into the Senate." He also repeatedly invoked the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, drawing a comparison between stopping El-Sayed from entering the Senate chamber and the passengers who fought back against the hijackers aboard United Flight 93.   El-Sayed, who would become the nation's first Muslim senator if elected, has called attacks on his loyalty to the country "shameful" and repeatedly denied any ties to extremist groups. The Republican president's remarks were condemned by Bishara Bahbah, a founder of Arab Americans for Trump, the group that helped lead the president's outreach to Arab American voters in 2024.   
   "The president's statements are out of line," he said in a phone interview. "They are crossing a red line. They are racist."   With Republicans on the defensive over inflation, soaring fuel prices and the Iran war, the president has been trying to generate turnout by claiming that El-Sayed and other Democrats are existential threats to America, instead of electoral rivals. Michigan's Senate race between El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers is among a handful of contests that could determine control of the chamber.   Trump made his remarks in Port Huron, a Canadian border city about an hour north of Detroit and near communities where he made significant gains among Arab American voters in 2024. He became the first Republican presidential candidate since 2000 to win Dearborn, a city with one of the nation's largest concentrations of Arab Americans.   Trump, who imposed a travel ban targeting several predominantly Muslim countries during his first term, has increasingly leaned into anti-Muslim rhetoric as Election Day approaches. He also attacked Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota at Sunday's rally, where he declared that he had come to Michigan "to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator."   Responding to Trump, who also regularly mocks his name, El-Sayed told supporters at a rally in Grand Rapids later Sunday that he doesn't care how Trump pronounces or misrepresents it.   
   "I don't even care that he remembers my whole name because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November," El-Sayed said, drawing cheers. "I will be Senator Muhammad to you, bro."   El-Sayed's faith, associations and past statements become campaign flashpoints   Central to Republicans' strategy against El-Sayed in the final weeks of the campaign has been an effort to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamic movement with branches that the U.S. government has designated as terrorist organizations.   There is no evidence that El-Sayed has any affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood. His half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, wrote on social media in 2012 that "my family has long been MB" and described a conversation with her mother about her involvement in the Muslim Brotherhood in the early 1970s.   El-Sayed was born in the United States to Egyptian immigrant parents who divorced when he was young. He was raised by his father, not his biological mother.   
   Trump on Sunday also targeted El-Sayed's ties to popular streamer Hasan Piker, who appeared alongside the Democrat multiple times during the primary campaign, including at his election night event.   Piker in the past has said that "Hamas is a thousand times better" than Israel, describing some Orthodox Jews as "inbred" and that "America deserved 9/11."   El-Sayed has faced criticism for his own rhetoric. He has repeatedly refused to answer questions about whether Iran or Israel poses a bigger threat to the country. Earlier this year, he said "hurt people hurt people" after an attack on a synagogue in the Detroit area. The attacker had lost four relatives in an Israeli airstrike on Lebanon the week earlier. El-Sayed later apologized, saying he was not trying to justify what happened.   "To anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful, I'm really sorry," he said. "That was not my intention."   
   Founder of Arab Americans for Trump calls the president 'racist'   Bahbah, whose organization has since changed its name to Arab Americans for Peace, said Trump's remarks were unacceptable to Arab and Muslim communities, including Christian Arabs.   "The remarks are out of line and crazy. I mean, no sane individual would say these things," Bahbah said.   Dearborn helped Trump win Michigan in 2024 after many voters in the city were outraged by the Biden administration's handling of the war in Gaza.   "The president of the United States saying that about a person because of his religion, that is just not acceptable," said Bahbah. "And people are going to remember that on Nov. 3."   Sen. Bernie Sanders, speaking at the Grand Rapids rally, said Trump and his allies were using Islamophobia because they have "nothing to say" about the issues most important to working people, such as health care, housing and income inequality.   "All they can do is foment hatred and divisiveness," Sanders said.   The campaign has been one of the most contentious this year   Rogers and El-Sayed have been locked in a bitter race to fill the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.   During their second and final general election campaign debate, Rogers questioned El-Sayed's loyalty to the United States.   "Are you for America, or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?" Rogers asked.   El-Sayed said that questioning was "shameful."   "I'm proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray," he said.   Speaking before Trump's appearance Sunday, Rogers repeated his allegations linking El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood.   "The Muslim Brotherhood celebrated exactly one victory in the United States in the primary this year," Rogers said on stage. "Abdul El-Sayed's."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                President Donald Trump listens as Nicki Minaj speaks during a campaign rally at McMorran Place Sports and Entertainment Center, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026, in Port Huron, Mich.
                
                    Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
    

   
   Rally doesn't deliver a new economic handout, but gets boost from Minaj   Trump has routinely announced new investments in factories at his campaign rallies, but he did not do so as part of his speech in Michigan, a state defined by the auto industry.   
   The president instead repeated investments already being made by domestic automakers. Those automakers could see their finances slump if the president expands his trade war with Canada, which has been an essential partner for the U.S. automotive sector.   While it lacked a fresh promise for Michigan's economy, Trump's rally did deliver a bit of star power.   Rapper Nicki Minaj appeared on stage and urged people to get out and vote for the state's Republican ticket. Her appearance followed an awkward moment from Trump, who has increasingly been fixated on commenting about other people's body parts.   After praising the body of Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican in a close election contest, Trump turned his eye toward Minaj and commented on her posterior.   The president then signaled for Minaj to stand for the crowd and she did, after which Trump said, "I hope Nicki wasn't insulted, but we love Nicki. She's been with us for a long time."

title: Political consultant on the impact of Republicans' gerrymandering efforts
description: NPR's Leila Fadel speaks with political consultant Mike Madrid about how Republicans' gerrymandering efforts have backfired.
body:
NPR's Leila Fadel speaks with political consultant Mike Madrid about how Republicans' gerrymandering efforts have backfired.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    LEILA FADEL, HOST:  Let's take a closer look now at the impact of gerrymandering efforts with someone who's been a political consultant for both Republicans and Democrats. Mike Madrid has been studying Latino voters for 35 years, and he's the author of "The Latino Century." He teaches at the University of Southern California and the University of California, Irvine. Good morning, and welcome to the program.MIKE MADRID: Good morning. Thank you so much for having me.FADEL: So how does the GOP's redistricting playbook look to you now, given the latest polling?MADRID: Well, it appears to have been a colossal mistake. Virtually every demographic that the Republican Party was relying on to serve as a new foundation for their racial realignment strategy - this new MAGA coalition has been abandoning them for the better part of at least 18 months, if not more. And there does not seem to be a single demographic where they have consolidated or increased support, rendering most of those map lines basically useless when, in fact, outcomes are exactly what you're trying to draw for. And it appears that in many of those 17 races that have been redrawn for Republican advantage, you're going to see a loss - a Republican loss or extremely competitive positioning - not what the Republicans drew these maps for at all.FADEL: So you're saying that they made assumptions about ethnic groups and American voters that just didn't bear out?MADRID: That's a great way to put it. That's exactly what has happened here. Their assumptions were that these Latino voters, specifically - these new minority voters, as they would refer to them - have not been voting along traditional minority lines. And that's, frankly, for both parties. But at this moment, when the pervasiveness of economic problems is so acute, you are seeing Latinos rejecting both parties. And, of course, as Republicans are the party in power, they will be suffering the most at the hands of these voters that are now the last major swing voter in the country. And I think in a few short days, we're going to see something rather historic showing that this dummymander that Republicans drew for themselves is going to backfire spectacularly.FADEL: How are Latinos redefining political trends?MADRID: Well, there was always an assumption that demographics is destiny, frankly, by both sides of the aisle. This was an issue, a term that gained popularity during the Obama years, where the belief was that all nonwhite voters were somehow born with Democratic Party DNA, that they would always be anti-Republican voters.For the better part of a decade, what we've seen is this shift towards the Republican Party or, better said, away from the Democratic Party, culminating in the 2024 election, where Latinos split basically 50/50. But as I've been counseling, most of the data was suggesting that this is a dealignment, not a realignment. They're not shifting alliances or vote preferences towards the Republican Party. They're shifting their voting patterns away from the Democratic Party and now, in this environment, away from the Republican Party, rejecting both parties' failures to address an upwardly mobile economic pocketbook framework - policy set - that's providing any meaningful results. So as long as that continues, this dealignment is going to define American politics going forward.FADEL: As in they won't be voting for either party, or they're a true swing vote?MADRID: Well, a little bit of both, right? They're kind of one and the same. At least that's the way that manifests itself. But the party alliances is what I think is the most fascinating feature. You see both Black voters and white voters, non-college-educated working class of either race, tend to be extraordinarily loyal, very hyperpartisan. And the hyperpartisanship has defined American politics for at least 30, maybe 40, 50 years. Latino voters are rejecting that racial polarization.They are also the most likely to be independent voters moving away from both parties. Even though they may be registered in one party, their propensity to vote against that party or foreignly (ph) is extremely high. We're seeing vote shifts of over 20% in some cases right now in the 2026 midterms that are coming up, according to exit polls. That's the same size of historic shift we saw just two years ago in the opposite direction. So this seemingly anominous (ph) - excuse me - anomalous tendency to vote for or against either party is actually the whole reason, the whole purpose, the whole framework from which elections were set up for in the first place. And so they're rejecting this idea of partisanship and polarization and what it means to be a minority voter in America.FADEL: Political consultant Mike Madrid. thank you so much for your time.MADRID: Thanks so much for having me.

title: Blanche defends DOJ lawsuit blocking Alaska Senate results if Republican loses
description: President Trump walks past Attorney Gene
body:
President Trump walks past Attorney General Todd Blanche after speaking at a roundtable event in the East Room of the White House on Oct. 21.
                
                    Alex Brandon/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Alex Brandon/AP
    

   
   U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday defended his department's lawsuit seeking to stop Alaska from automatically certifying the results of its Senate election if the Republican incumbent there loses.   Earlier this week he had said the Justice Department could get involved in the vote certification process in a "doomsday" scenario.   
   Pressed on CNN about whether the suit was setting the stage for President Trump to challenge the outcome of next week's midterm elections, Blanche denied it.   The seat is seen as one vital for Republicans if they are to maintain control of the Senate for the second half of Trump's term in office.   The Justice Department claims that potential confusion over candidates with similar names is the reason for the suit, though some Democrats have argued that it is actually an attempt to interfere in the democratic process.   
   A ballot with two Sullivans   A candidate on the Nov. 3 ballot is a retired schoolteacher from Petersburg, named Daniel J. Sullivan, with a remarkably similar name to the current Republican senator, Dan Sullivan.   Republicans have accused Daniel J. Sullivan of running as a spoiler to try and divert votes away from the incumbent. But the other Sullivan has said the decision to run was his own and denied his candidacy was intended to confuse voters or siphon votes in Republican Sullivan's tight race against Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                This combination photo shows Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, left, in Palmer, Alaska, Aug. 17, 2026, and a candidate in Alaska's Senate race, Dan Sullivan, right, in Petersburg, Alaska, July 3, 2026.
                
                    Mark Thiessen; Becky Bohrer/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mark Thiessen; Becky Bohrer/AP
    

   
   The Justice Department has argued in its suit that the name overlap risks confusing voters.   "We're not laying any groundwork for the president to do that," Blanche told anchor Dana Bash on CNN's State of the Union, after she asked whether the administration was positioning Trump to overturn a result he did not like.   "President Trump is not trying to take over a state election in any way, shape or form," Blanche added.   Tense interview   The exchange grew heated when Bash raised Blanche's "doomsday" remark to reporters in Virginia.   Bash asked Blanche whether the Alaska case risked repeating some of the events during the aftermath of the 2020 election and the Jan. 6 attacks on the Capitol. "Oh, you got to stop it with that. You are not being a real person. Come on, man," Blanche replied, calling the suggestion "crazy."   
   The Justice Department's lawsuit has demanded that Alaska not "certify any election results that may be impacted by voter confusion." Blanche insisted the more precise demand for relief from the Justice Department is "to not certify if the law is broken," and that it would ultimately be a question for Alaska and its courts to settle.   Blanche suggested it was "so embarrassing" for CNN that the discussion had turned to Jan. 6, and framed the case as a test of whether Alaska had violated federal law and the Constitution by permitting such a potentially confusing ballot process to continue.   "It is an obligation of the states to avoid confusion, among other things, confusion in the minds of voters in the election process," he said.   A state court and the Alaska Supreme Court kept Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot, after Republican election officials in Alaska had sought to remove him on the grounds that his candidacy was to mislead voters intentionally. That Alaska court decision, Blanche said, "explicitly didn't consider federal law."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Democrat Mary Peltola smiles ahead of a debate with Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska's Senate race, Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, in Anchorage, Alaska.
                
                    Becky Bohrer/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Becky Bohrer/AP
    

   
   Trump claims responsibility   The suit was filed late Thursday in federal court in Alaska and, citing the National Voter Registration Act, asked for certification to be blocked after the election until the government has investigated whether votes for Daniel J. Sullivan were indeed intended for the senator.   The Department of Justice has not clarified how that determination could be made in light of the secret nature of the ballot, but Trump said Friday that he ordered the case. "I'm the one that said do it," he told reporters in Florida.   
   Sen. Lisa Murkowski, Alaska's other Republican senator and a backer of her colleague Sullivan's reelection, said on social media that the state had already distinguished the candidates and that the department should not have sued.   State officials have already moved to distinguish the two men, with the senator appearing as "Dan S. Sullivan," marked as a registered Republican and the incumbent. Meanwhile "Daniel J. Sullivan Jr." carries no party label beside his name.   Alaska's ranked choice system also allows voters to rank both candidates, and back in August during the state's primary, the senator won more than 68,000 votes to the other Sullivan's 4,107.   
   The lawsuit was signed by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, who had represented several people accused of participating in the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol before he joined the department.

title: Democrats see an opportunity to tilt Pennsylvania's state legislature their way
description: Statehouse elections this fall could swing the balance of power in state capitals. In Pennsylvania, Democrats could take control of what has be
body:
Statehouse elections this fall could swing the balance of power in state capitals. In Pennsylvania, Democrats could take control of what has been a divided legislature.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:  In addition to the congressional votes in just over a week, more than 6,100 seats are up for election in state legislatures. States make most of the laws on education, taxes, reproductive rights, crime and social media access, among other things. Democrats say they see opportunities to tilt some legislatures their way this year, like in Pennsylvania, where the legislature is divided - for now. Carmen Russell-Sluchansky of member station WHYY joins us from the road in Harrisburg. Welcome.CARMEN RUSSELL-SLUCHANSKY, BYLINE: Thank you, Ayesha.RASCOE: Can you lay out kind of the landscape for us? Who controls most state legislatures?RUSSELL-SLUCHANSKY: Well, across 50 states, 28 have Republicans controlling both chambers while Democrats control 18 legislatures. A few legislatures, like the one here in Pennsylvania, are divided. Now, to fully understand how important the balance of power is, I talked to John Kennedy. He's a political science professor at Westchester University. He says even though races for Congress and governor get a lot of the attention, the down-ballot ones are equally important, if not more so.JOHN KENNEDY: The fact of the matter in the day-in, day-out basis is state governments, state lawmakers, state governors have a greater impact on our everyday lives than what takes place in Washington, D.C.RUSSELL-SLUCHANSKY: He noted that the shift toward Republicans stems from the 2010 midterm cycle when they largely swept state legislatures, and that gave them the power to solidify their holds through redistricting.RASCOE: OK. Well, let's use Pennsylvania as an example. What difference would it make if power does or doesn't shift?RUSSELL-SLUCHANSKY: I mean, it could be a massive difference here. Democrats haven't controlled the legislature here for over 30 years. Governor Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, has laid out what he says Democrats will do if they win legislative control and he's reelected.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)JOSH SHAPIRO: We're going to raise the minimum wage to $15 an hour in the commonwealth. I'll tell you what else we're going to do. We're going to build more affordable housing and take on those utility companies that keep jacking up our rates here in Pennsylvania.RUSSELL-SLUCHANSKY: Now, his challenger, Republican state treasurer Stacy Garrity, says Shapiro shouldn't blame the Republicans for not getting things done already.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)STACY GARRITY: The governor has consistently said - used the excuse that he can't do anything because he has a divided legislature. Well, that's not what real leadership is. Real leadership - they call the leaders to the table, and you negotiate.RUSSELL-SLUCHANSKY: By the way, you know, some Republicans I've talked to have hoped, even if Garrity doesn't win, she will be a strong enough candidate to protect those down the ballot races.RASCOE: It seems clear these are important races. But are people actually paying attention to them?RUSSELL-SLUCHANSKY: You know, it's just not on as many people's radars as the congressional races or the race for governor. For example, I went to a farmers market in Wrightstown and met Jerry Scupp (ph), an independent voter in a very contested state senate district. He didn't know the candidates, like a lot of people.JERRY SCUPP: I have to say that I'm not as tuned in as that.RUSSELL-SLUCHANSKY: Several other people I talked to said they just plan to vote on party lines. Yet there is a lot of money going into these local races. So for example, in Bucks County, Scupp's district, more than $7 million has been spent, and a lot of that is going to ads in which they're criticizing each other's positions on data centers, which has been a hot-button topic. And that's one of maybe only four toss-up districts, three in the Philly suburbs.RASCOE: Outside of Pennsylvania, are there other states that could flip?RUSSELL-SLUCHANSKY: Yeah. I mean, Democrats are pouring millions and millions of dollars into trying to flip chambers around the country, especially Wisconsin, Michigan, Minnesota, Arizona, New Hampshire, as well as Pennsylvania. Also it's not just about trying to flip districts. In some states, Democrats are simply looking to reduce Republican power or break the supermajorities they have that prevent Democratic governors from vetoing their bills, like in North Carolina and Kansas. I reached out to the national Republican group that works on these races. They didn't respond, but they have tried to highlight things like democratic socialists running in some of the states, and they have acknowledged that they're largely playing defense this year.RASCOE: That's WHYY's Carmen Russell-Sluchansky. Thank you so much for joining us.RUSSELL-SLUCHANSKY: Thank you, Ayesha.

title: The rise of the economic populist: What voters want from both parties this year
description: A new kind of economic populism is surging in both parties this year as voters search for a political party that can solve growing concerns abo
body:
A new kind of economic populism is surging in both parties this year as voters search for a political party that can solve growing concerns about financial stability.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT SIMON, HOST:  Right-wing populism in the U.S. once meant being against the socially liberal elites on the East Coast and in California. On the left, populism used to mean being against billionaires and big corporations. But in this midterm election, those definitions are getting scrambled and a new kind of economic populism may be converging from the left and the right. NPR's senior national political correspondent Mara Liasson has this report.MARA LIASSON, BYLINE: You'd be forgiven if you thought the following ads were run by Democrats.(SOUNDBITE OF MONTAGE)FRENCH HILL: Keep Wall Street from buying up our neighborhoods.MIKE ROGERS: The pharmaceutical companies are ripping American families off.JOE MITCHELL: Because politicians shouldn't get rich while Iowa families struggle to afford groceries, housing and childcare.LIASSON: They sound like they were written by Bernie Sanders' media consultant, but French Hill, Mike Rogers and Joe Mitchell are all Republicans. Historians of populism, like Georgetown professor Michael Kazin, say Americans are more open to economic populism when they're feeling squeezed or worse.MICHAEL KAZIN: Economic populism emerges when ordinary people believe that they're getting screwed, betrayed by economic elites.LIASSON: This year's populism is bipartisan. It's why you see Steve Bannon and Bernie Sanders appear back-to-back at the same anti-AI conference, and it's reflected in poll after poll. Democratic pollster Celinda Lake surveyed 500 working-class Americans without college degrees and with incomes under $150,000. The poll was commissioned by the Friedrich Ebert Foundation, which is affiliated with the German Social Democratic Party.CELINDA LAKE: What really surprises us is the number of people - about 40% - who are cynical about the American dream don't think it's possible anymore and are sarcastic about it, that it's gone. It's a lie. It's a false promise.LIASSON: A false promise that if you worked hard and got an education, you could do as well or better than your parents. What also surprised Lake was that big majorities, 70%, blame extreme wealth inequality for ending the American dream. And the same big majorities, 69%, say the government has an obligation to address it. NPR's swing voter focus groups found the same thing. All our voters backed Biden in 2020, and then they all voted for Trump in 2024. They agreed to be part of the focus group on the condition that they would be identified by first name only. So here's Jennifer (ph), Tony (ph) and Jeff (ph).JENNIFER: It seems like the most wealth in this country is held by such a small percentage of people. And then we have people, you know, really struggling, and I think it's getting harder and harder to reach that American dream and get where you need to be.TONY: I have nothing against billionaires or people who are making money. But I think that a lot of our problems, economic problems, are stemming from those who can't get enough who don't want to pay taxes.JEFF: There's a handful of people, maybe 10 people, that hold 50% of the wealth in the country. And if you do have that much money, you should be taxed heavily, and that should trickle down to everyday citizens.LIASSON: Our focus groups reflect what national polls have shown. A recent Wall Street Journal survey showed majority support for a lot of economic populist proposals previously identified with Democrats, including capping the cost of prescription drugs, childcare and credit card interest, higher taxes on the rich and Medicare for All. The big political question is which party can take advantage of this new openness to government action to address the cost of living, especially at a time, says Michael Kazin, when people are afraid.KAZIN: It's not just discontent about the president. I think the fear of the future. That's part of the fear about AI. It's part of the fear about China becoming the dominant economic power. So whichever party is able to say, look, we have an idea of how the government can help you have a better life and help your children have a better life. I think that party has a chance of becoming the dominant party.LIASSON: Celinda Lake thinks this is an opportunity for Democrats, since they're still seen as the party that protects working people, not corporations. But republicans see opportunities, too. Oren Cass is the chief economist at American Compass.OREN CASS: American Compass is a think tank founded to work on the direction of the right of center after the Trump presidency.LIASSON: Cass points to Republicans like Missouri Senator Josh Hawley, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who all talk about a new kind of economics. They call it covenant economics or common good capitalism.CASS: What you've had really going on more than a decade now is on the right of center, a shift away from the kind of libertarian fundamentalism that people have come to think of as conservative. You know, smaller government is always better.LIASSON: Donald Trump made it safe for Republicans to reconsider conservative economic policy, replacing his party's orthodoxy on free trade and immigration with tariffs and deportations. He promised to protect Social Security and Medicare. His government has intervened directly in the economy, taking an ownership stake in more than 30 private companies. Although at the same time, Trump also cut taxes for the wealthy, enriched himself and his family and shrunk the social safety net.Celinda Lake and Oren Cass each think their party has the best chance to find the new sweet spot in American politics. More liberal on economics than Republicans are now, more conservative on social issues than Democrats. And the political prize could be a very big one. Instead of one super close election after another that produces only gridlock, the party that figures out the new economic populism could create a functioning, durable majority. In the meantime, says Celinda Lake, populism will keep shaking up American politics.LAKE: You're going to see populist candidates emerge on the left and the right, and you're going to also see more volatility. And you're going to see more outsiders be elected because of the power of this message and the emotion behind it.LIASSON: Mara Liasson, NPR News.(SOUNDBITE OF SURPRISE CHEF'S "ALL NEWS IS GOOD NEWS")

title: Redistricting isn't playing out how the GOP hoped. And, Brazil's Lula wins 4th term
description:
GOP Redistricting Bust, Lula Wins Brazil Election, Protest Spread In Europe
    
            
                
                Transcrip
body:
GOP Redistricting Bust, Lula Wins Brazil Election, Protest Spread In Europe
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-149917/nx-s1-mx-6016798-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                North Carolina Republican Congressional candidates, State Rep. Jennifer Balkcom and Laurie Buckhout (R) are embraced by President Trump during an election rally on October 20, 2026 in Greenville, North Carolina. Buckhout is running in North Carolina's 1st District which was redrawn to heavily favor Republicans and is now a toss-up.
                
                    Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
    

   
   Republicans had a plan to keep control of the House in the midterms: Redraw congressional district lines to favor the GOP and avoid the historical pattern of heavy midterm losses. President Trump began pressuring Republican-led states to do just that last year, but it isn't working out as expected. Republicans could now be spending millions of dollars on House seats that were supposed to be easy wins, and end up losing anyway. Of the 15 districts drawn specifically to favor Republicans, only five are rated by the Cook Political Report as either likely or solid Republican. Most are toss-ups or lean toward a Democratic win.   🎧 One reason the Republicans' redistricting push hasn't been as successful as expected is that some district lines were drawn based on the 2024 Trump electorate, NPR's Tamara Keith tells Up First. Since then, his support has weakened, particularly among young and Latino voters. Several Democratic incumbents targeted by redistricting have stuck it out to fight for their seats. A Republican strategist involved with midterm races, but who wasn't authorized to speak publicly, pushed back on the characterization that redistricting didn't work, saying that it "creates new battlefields" but doesn't "create outcomes."➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.   
   In a stunning political comeback, leftist Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in the presidential runoff election in Brazil. Lula defeated Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, by more than 4 million votes. It's the first time since Brazil restored democracy in 1989 that a candidate who finished second in the first round has gone on to win the presidency.   🎧 Lula's win appears to have put the brake on a right-wing sweep in Latin America, NPR's Carrie Kahn says. Seven conservative presidents have been elected in the past 18 months. Kahn says one message helped rally voters in the final weeks of Lula's campaign: that the return of a Bolsonaro to power would be an existential threat to Brazilian democracy.   Large demonstrations against the government continued over the weekend in France, where more than 100,000 people showed up in Paris, and more than 400,000 came out nationwide. What started with students demanding better conditions has grown into a much bigger movement. Unions and public-sector workers have joined, calling for more public spending and protesting growing inequality. Similar protests have erupted across Europe, from Spain to Serbia.   🎧 The reasons behind the protests vary, from schools and housing costs to corruption, NPR's Eleanor Beardsley says. But they have something in common: most are leaderless movements by young people frustrated with the world they're being left to. In Serbia, crowds celebrated in the streets of Belgrade after a student-led movement known as the "student-list" defeated the party of longtime strongman Aleksandar Vucic in Sunday's parliamentary elections. The win followed two years of protests over government corruption and lack of accountability.   
   Healthcare helpline   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        Oona Zenda/KFF Health News
    

   
   Out-of-pocket maternity expenses are difficult to predict. A federal requirement for insurers to provide personalized cost estimates under the No Surprises Act was supposed to take effect in 2022, but federal regulators haven't made it happen despite pressure from Congress. Until the cost of maternity care gets more transparent, here are some tips to help you budget for the cost of pregnancy:   👶 Enroll your baby in your insurance before your deadline. For most employer health plans, that's within 30 days of birth.👶 Check what your maximum out-of-pocket expense is. That's the most you'll pay each year for covered, in-network expenses before your insurance pays 100% of the costs.👶 Choose in-network providers whenever possible.👶 Go over every bill, and don't be afraid to appeal errors.👶 Ask your hospital or other providers about financial assistance.   Deep dive   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                A satellite image provided by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) shows Hurricane Isaias approaching the Gulf Coast of Alabama and Florida on Friday, Oct. 9 2026.
                
                    National Oceanic and Atmospheric/National Oceanic and Atmospheric
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        National Oceanic and Atmospheric/National Oceanic and Atmospheric
    

   
   When Hurricane Isaias made landfall in Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 storm, Google DeepMind's AI model outperformed the traditional model, correctly predicting it would hit the Florida Panhandle rather than head west toward Louisiana. Hurricane forecasters say they're increasingly relying on AI technology, and that it's rapidly transforming the field.   🌀 The National Hurricane Center first started incorporating Google DeepMind into its official forecasts last year. By the end of the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season, it was among the best at predicting a storm's strength and path.🌀 Traditional physics-based prediction models use real-time atmospheric data like temperature, humidity, pressure and wind shear. AI models rely more on history and patterns from analyzing thousands of past storms.🌀 AI models can feel like a black box; meteorologists depend on them but don't always know why their predictions are correct.🌀 Humans still interpret the results of these models and translate them into clear guidance people can act on.   3 things to know before you go   The latest edition of NPR's Breakfast Around the World series takes us to the ancient city of Aleppo in northern Syria, where a sweet semolina pudding called mamounieh evokes memories both bitter and sweet.The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported 4,588 confirmed measles cases across the U.S. this year through Oct. 22 — more than double the number for all of 2025. Cases are particularly high in Pennsylvania.The general fertility rate for U.S. women fell by 1% to a record low in 2025, according to the CDC. Birth rates declined among women in their 20s but rose among women ages 30 to 45.   
   This newsletter was edited by Majd Al-Waheidi.

title: Independent candidates sense a moment. Some Democrats hope they're right
description: Pins and bumper stickers supporting Dan
body:
Pins and bumper stickers supporting Dan Osborn's candidacy for U.S. Senate sit on a campaign table on Sept. 3 at Pals Brewing Company in North Platte, Neb. Osborn, a 51-year-old Navy veteran, is running as an independent.
                
                    Austin Johnson/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Austin Johnson/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   BURWELL, Neb. — Tucked in the rolling Sandhills, the largest sand dune formation in America, sits Morgan Ranch, a 15,000-acre, family-run operation home to 1,000 cows and thousands of offspring.   "There's a lot of mouths to feed — both animals and two-legged," laughed Dan Morgan. His ranch has one of the largest privately owned Wagyu herds in the U.S.   He said his job has given him a front row seat to what he calls the "uncertainty" of President Trump's policies.   "To raise a piece of meat takes me three years," Morgan said. "Well, look at the changes in the past two years: costs, tariffs, reciprocal tariffs because half of our business is export — it's just hell," he said.   
   He's a Democrat — a self-described small blue dot in a sea of red, in a county and state that Trump dominated two years ago.   
   There's no Democrat running for the Senate in Nebraska, but Morgan is excited by independent candidate Dan Osborn.   "Osborn makes the case that somebody needs to represent the working family," Morgan said. "And he can effectively do that."   Osborn is one of four independents running for Senate in states President Trump won handily, including Idaho, South Dakota and Montana. Buoyed by the president's sinking approval ratings and public frustration over affordability, independent candidates argue they bring a winning case to voters.    It is an argument that some Democrats hope will resonate with voters as the party looks to retake control of Congress, betting that these candidates can help topple Republicans in parts of the country where their own brand is hurting.    "I'm a partisan Democrat. I believe in the Democratic Party. I also believe in building coalitions so we can win elections and then do the work of the people," said Jane Kleeb, the chair of the Nebraska Democratic Party. "And if that means creating coalitions with independents in some of our states, then that's exactly what we need to do."   
   But while these independents are generally unified in their political philosophy that the two-party system is toxic and has led to legislative intransigence, the challenges they face in their respective races are different, in large part because of the role the Democratic Party has decided to play.   "Spoiler" accusations abound in Montana   Seth Bodnar, a former Green Beret running for Senate in Montana, said voters he talks to are fed up with politics as usual — and that he offers a viable alternative as an independent.   "When I go to Washington, D.C., I'm not going to put on a red jersey with an 'R' or a blue jersey with a 'D.' I'm going to have a jersey with an 'M' on it, and I'm going to work for Montana," Bodnar said in an interview from the homecoming parade at the University of Montana, where he used to be president.   Like Osborn, Bodnar said if elected, he won't caucus with either party. The current two independents in the Senate, Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Angus King of Maine, both caucus with Democrats.   His theory of the case is that in a closely divided Senate, an independent willing to work with either party — but beholden to neither — actually holds significant strength.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Seth Bodnar, an independent candidate for a U.S. Senate seat in Montana, speaks to supporters and the press outside the Yellowstone County Courthouse, Aug. 7, in Billings, Mont.
                
                    Mathew Brown/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mathew Brown/AP
    

   
   "I think there is real power in an independent or multiple independents that can work together, even with people who maybe don't leave their caucus but form an independent-minded bloc, that can move forward common sense solutions that this country so desperately needs," Bodnar said.   The race has been marked by frustration among Democrats — at either Bodnar for not running as a Democrat himself, or at the Democratic nominee, Alani Bankhead, for not dropping out and creating a glide path for Bodnar.   "Had Bodnar run as a Democrat, he'd be leading in this election," said former Democratic Gov. Brian Schweitzer.   
   "At the end of the day, there will be a lot of people that look in the mirror and say, 'Oh, my God, if we would have just run a Democrat without an independent, we would have won this election,'" Schweitzer said.   
   Many prominent Montana Democrats — like former Sen. Jon Tester and former Gov. Steve Bullock — have endorsed Bodnar, setting up a divide between Democrats supporting their own party's nominee and those supporting the independent.   "It's just been really, really contentious and quite a bitter thing within the state party," said Rob Saldin, political science professor at the University of Montana.   Saldin said unlike states like Idaho, which has deep Republican entrenchment, Montana Democrats aren't as "beat down" and look at the election as a chance to rebuild the brand in the state.   "They want somebody who, for years into the future, is going to be able to help bring money into the state Democratic Party, to help down-ballot candidates for the legislature, to be the face of the party in the state," he said. "And when you've got an independent candidate who's saying, 'a pox on both your houses,' this is not the guy who's going to be able to do that work in the trenches for the party."   There was an effort to get Bankhead to exit the race before the August deadline. Bankhead said she and her family were harassed. She also said "white gloved politicians" were subtly trying to tell her to drop out of the race.    
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Alani Bankhead, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Montana, is seen preparing for a rally in East Helena, Mont. on Aug. 10, 2026 — the last day that ballots could be changed. Bankhead verified she was not dropping out of the race.
                
                    Clayton Murphy/Montana Public Radio
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Clayton Murphy/Montana Public Radio
    

   
   "They were very polite. They didn't ask me to drop out, but it was subtle — like, 'Well, what's the goal and what kind of job do you want down the road?'" she said, adding she heard from a sitting senator, sitting governor and former cabinet official. "Nobody from the [Democratic National Committee] was like, 'drop out' but that was certainly the nudge."   
   Bankhead claimed in an interview with Montana PBS that she was offered a DNC job if she dropped out of the race. The DNC denies this.   Bankhead said if Democrats want to support independents — there's a better way to do it.   "Nebraska was very transparent, right? The Democratic nominee said they would step aside in favor of the independent if the people voted for them. And that's very transparent — that's great."   Fending off "Democrat Dan" label in Nebraska   Kleeb, the Nebraska Democratic Party chair and a DNC vice chair, said Nebraska Democrats were very conscious about being transparent regarding their intentions to support the independent on the ticket.   "We were very honest with voters," said Kleeb. "And I think if you're going to do this as a Democratic Party, that's what you have to do — you have to be honest with voters, explain the strategy and make sure that Democrats support that."   She said Democrats had high hopes for Osborn, a mechanic who got his start in politics leading a strike at the Kellogg's plant in 2021, and raised eyebrows two years ago when he came within seven points of incumbent Republican Sen. Deb Fischer.   The choice for Democrats to support Osborn led to the party running someone in the primary with the stated intention of having her drop out to clear the path for Osborn. There was then a lawsuit attempting to force the party to replace that winning primary candidate who dropped out.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Dan Osborn, an independent candidate for U.S. Senate from Nebraska, speaks with Maranda Lee, co-owner of Lee's Crossroads Cafe, at the cafe after a town hall meeting Sept. 3, in Arapahoe, Neb.
                
                    Austin Johnson/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Austin Johnson/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Kleeb said the decision to back Osborn is part of a long-term goal, which includes repairing the damage to the Democratic brand in a redder state like Nebraska.   "It's right that people have pushed back on our brand — it's a problem. We are working on it," Kleeb said, adding there will be a time when Nebraska builds up its Democratic base so it's competitive statewide.   
   In the meantime, Democrats like Kleeb are hoping Osborn can help the party deny Republicans a majority in the Senate.   Osborn has been crisscrossing the state on a 93-county tour. His town halls have a distinctly populist pitch to voters denouncing money in politics.   
   "We are at a turning point in our country where we have to take it back for ourselves — for the workers, for the people," he said to a group of 30 in Taylor. "Because the powers that be — the money interests — have taken control."   In between stops in five counties on one day, Osborn said in an interview he's not only running against incumbent GOP Sen Pete Ricketts.   "I'm running against the entire establishment that is stuck in this system that's working exactly the way it's supposed to work for them," he said. "I represent something that's going to throw a wrench in."   As Osborn travels the state, Ricketts has been working to convince constituents that the independent is actually a Democrat.   "Dan's a Democrat. Open borders, take our guns, higher taxes, that's no fun — vote for Osborn and you'll see, the Democrats will run D.C.," croons a radio ad from the Ricketts campaign. In their debate, Ricketts called Osborn "Democrat Dan" so many times the independent suggested they should bring out a third podium.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                This 2010 photo shows the Sandhills in north central Nebraska. Independent candidate Dan Osborn, who's running for U.S. Senate, recently held a series of meet and greets and town halls in the Sandhills, trying to form a broad coalition of Republicans and Democrats alike.
                
                    Nati Harnik/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Nati Harnik/AP
    

   
   Sue McNeil, a lifelong Republican voter in Loup County, said she doesn't like the nickname.   "I think they're just using that 'Democrat Dan' to scare people, because Nebraska is a Republican state and I feel like a lot of people are a little nervous about supporting a Democrat," she said. "But Dan Osborn is not a Democrat — he's an independent."   She's supporting Osborn, citing frustration with the Trump administration and GOP-controlled Congress.   "Why did we start the war with Iran? Our fuel prices have skyrocketed," she said, noting she recently paid $159 to fill up the pickup. "How are we supposed to make it?"   
   But other conservative voters say they agree with Ricketts.   "Osborn is a fraud," said Rich Sherbeck from Ansley. "He's not really an independent — he's a Democrat, DSA-aligned."   Casey Stengel, who said he always votes Republican, was curious about Osborn and came to a meet and greet at a coffee shop in Thedford. He told Osborn he was on the fence and asked him to convince him to vote for him.   Osborn launched into a discussion about uplifting workers and building bridges with both parties to bring about real change.   Once Osborn left, Stengel sighed.   "Yes, there's good ideas," he said. "But we all know one man ain't going to go fix the deal."   Sam Gringlas contributed to this report.

title: Republicans are spending millions and still may not win districts drawn to favor them
body:
North Carolina Republican congressional candidates state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom and Laurie Buckhout (right) are embraced by President Trump during an election rally on Oct. 20, 2026, in Greenville, N.C. Buckhout is running in North Carolina's 1st District, which was redrawn to heavily favor Republicans and is now a toss-up.
                
                    Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
    

   
   📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App      Starting last year, President Trump and his political team put pressure on Republican-led states to redraw congressional district lines to favor Republicans. It was supposed to build a firewall for Republicans hoping to avoid the historical pattern of heavy midterm losses for the president's party.   "It just has not turned out that way," said Nathan Gonzales, editor of Inside Elections.   Instead, Republicans are spending millions of dollars on House seats that were supposed to deliver easy wins and may end up losing them anyway.   
   Among those districts is North Carolina's 1st Congressional District, which the state legislature aggressively redrew late last year to try to make it a reliably Republican district. Under the new lines, Trump would have won the district by more than 11 percentage points in 2024. Now it is widely considered a toss up.   
   Trump recently headlined a rally in eastern North Carolina where former Republican Party chairman turned U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley got most of the attention.   It was cold and getting late when Trump finally got around to mentioning two congressional candidates sitting in the VIP section.   "Come up. The two of you, we have to get them in," Trump said of Laurie Buckhout, the Republican nominee in NC-01 and Jennifer Balkcom, the Republican running to represent NC-11 on the opposite side of the state. "We have to vote for them. These are two special people. Come on up."   On stage, Buckhout, a retired Army colonel, who ran and lost in the district two years ago, leaned into the partisan advantage Republicans should have in the district, saying it's "simple math."    "There are more of us," said Buckhout. "All you've got to do is get out the vote. God bless you, Mr. President."   
   But concern about turnout is exactly why Trump was in the state, begging voters to cast their ballots as if he were on it. Trump told the rally crowd that House Speaker Mike Johnson had asked him to give an extra boost to Buckhout and Balkcom, describing the situation as "tough."   "He said 'if you could, give them a special call out tonight, because they're going to have close races'," Trump said.   Buckhout and her team didn't respond to requests to participate in this story. But, if this redraw was meant to notch an easy Republican win, it hasn't worked out. This is now one of the most expensive House races in the country, with more than $42 million spent on advertising between Sept. 1 and Election Day, according to an NPR analysis of AdImpact data.   New district lines, same issues   
            
        
            
            
            
        


        
                A volunteer snaps a photo of Democratic Rep. Don Davis with Onslow County Board of Commissioner candidates Rebecca Cooper and Michel Leandre Jr. outside an early voting location in Swansboro, N.C. Onslow is one of six counties added to North Carolina's 1st District in the latest redraw of congressional district lines.
                hide caption
            
            
   
   One recent morning, Democratic Rep. Don Davis, was greeting voters at an early voting location in Swansboro, at the far southeastern tip of the district, an area he hasn't represented before.   As Davis introduced himself to a voter walking out of the polling place, the man told him he wasn't in his district.   "Oh, I'm sorry," Davis said, laughing and noting this has been happening to him a lot lately.   "This is my third run on a third new map," said Davis.   
   Davis has been a top target for Republicans in multiple rounds of redistricting. This time his home county was drawn out of the district and he got all or part of six new counties. He says issues in eastern North Carolina, though, are universal.    "You hear so much about affordability, inflation and costs but I believe this is becoming for many about survivability," said Davis, referencing farmers, truckers and fishermen hit by high fuel prices. "Just how they're able to make it and survive during these tough times."   
   Davis is a happy warrior, even joking about his predicament with a volunteer handing out flyers in front of the polling place.   "I just don't know how many other ways you could redraw it now, other than maybe, you know if you just start annexing Virginia or something or maybe taking it into the Atlantic Ocean or something," he said adding with a laugh, "I'll just swim and talk to the fish, you know."   Republicans and Democrats alike acknowledge Davis is a formidable campaigner, making this race more competitive than it should be just based on the way the lines were drawn.   "I think they believed that they had beaten Don Davis with the redistricting pen," said Morgan Jackson, a prominent North Carolina political consultant, who is running Democrat Roy Cooper's U.S. Senate campaign. "As it turns out, Don Davis has always been a tough out. He's a local politician who runs really strong."   
   Incumbent Democrats in several redrawn districts around the country decided to stay in and fight and now look well positioned to win, said Inside Election's Gonzales.   "Republicans gained an advantage in 15 congressional districts nationwide but what we are seeing this close to Election Day is that some of those that were supposed to be easy victories are not turning out that way and the party is having to pour in millions of dollars to win districts that were supposed to be easy victories," said Gonzales.   A Republican strategist involved with midterm races, but who wasn't authorized to speak publicly, pushed back on the idea that the redistricting push has been a bust, saying "redistricting creates new battlefields, it doesn't create outcomes." That's a lot less confidence than Republicans were projecting about these districts just a few months ago.   Two Florida congressional districts redrawn to boot Democratic incumbents are nearing a combined $90 million in ad spending. In Texas, districts drawn to have a 10-point Trump advantage have shifted toward Democrats and a previously safe Republican district that had some Democratic voters added to it in the redrawn maps now appears to be at risk as well.   
   "I think at the end of the day, this will go down as a dummymander rather than a gerrymander," said Jackson.

title: In Arkansas, Democrats see an opening at the edge of the competitive midterms map
body:
Arkansas Democratic Senate nominee Hallie Shoffner speaks with voters at a campaign stop in Hope, Ark. Friday, Oct. 23, 2026.
                
                    Stephen Fowler/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Stephen Fowler/NPR
    

   
   HOPE, Ark. — For Senate candidate Hallie Shoffner, the most important political label she wears isn't that she's a Democrat. Or that she's not a Republican. Instead, it's that she is an Arkansan.   As a lunchtime crowd ate at Tailgater's Burger Company Friday, Shoffner decried what she called a historically unproductive Congress driven by extreme voices in each party and pitched herself to receptive — if skeptical — voters as a candidate who would better serve their needs.   Arkansas is one of the most conservative states in the country, with nearly two out of three voters supporting President Trump in 2024 and Republican Sen. Tom Cotton in 2020.   
   But in the final days of the 2026 midterm election, Shoffner and other Arkansas Democrats are crisscrossing the state with a message that seeks to capitalize on the Trump administration's unpopularity, stubbornly high prices and anti-incumbency vibes.   "We're the sleeper race," Shoffner told NPR. "I mean, we're the race that no one's noticed and that no one is going to see coming."   Republicans have taken some notice, pre-emptively pouring millions of dollars into the Senate race, the Little Rock-based 2nd Congressional District and robust get-out-the vote efforts to try and stem the rising tide of dissatisfaction with the party.   But even in a midterm cycle where Senate races in states like Kansas, Iowa, Ohio and Texas are viewed as tossups, and where the landscape of potentially competitive House races stretches deep into conservative territory, Arkansas seems a bridge too far for election forecasters.   Arkansas' 2nd Congressional District is considered "Likely Republican," according to the Cook Political Report, and its Senate race is "Solid Republican."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Hallie Shoffner, the Democratic Senate nominee in Arkansas, has emphasized her farming background and belief that both parties have ignored the people's needs in the state.
                
                    Stephen Fowler/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Stephen Fowler/NPR
    

   
   Arkansas First   At an outdoor coffee shop in Arkadelphia, Vanilla Hannah said she was there to support Shoffner and talk about her own reelection bid to be a local justice of the peace. She said it's possible that Arkansas could elect Democrats this year because the crop of candidates seems willing to work with people to meet their needs — and there are a lot of them.   
   "When it comes down to basic needs or whatever, the 'D' or the 'R' after your name don't mean a thing, because we're all suffering and all having the same issues and everybody's ready for a change," she said. "And running for an election is not just running specifically on the Democratic policies or the Republican or the libertarians or whatever. It's just what you believe in, and it seems like more and more people are having a common belief now."   Later, Shoffner visited a small family farm in nearby Bierne where several members of the Hatley family cooked sorghum to make syrup and talked about why they were supporting her campaign.    
   Shoffner is a multigenerational farmer who decided to shut down her family's operation in 2025, citing financial headwinds from rising input costs and Trump administration tariff and trade policies. That in turn inspired her Senate run and influenced much of her campaign's focus.   Sliding behind the wheel of a side-by-side utility vehicle, Shoffner takes off across the property and recounts her life story that led her away from the farm, into nonprofit work and back home when her dad got sick.   She doesn't buy the argument that her chances are low to win.   "This race isn't about Democrats or Republicans or independents or any of that," she said. "This isn't some kind of weird political alignment, this is a values alignment. This is reorienting representation in Arkansas based on common sense, based on compassion and based on showing up."   She said national Republicans — and Democrats — have made the mistake of ignoring the needs of Arkansas residents, especially with agriculture and trade policies.   "I come from a place, a community, that died in my lifetime," she said. "I was the last one left and I felt left behind. I felt like no one was really talking to me or talking about me. I felt like folks were making decisions about me, but without me, and ultimately they were rewriting the rules."   
   Now, with record diesel prices, the war in Iran and tariffs, Shoffner said she believes that Arkansas voters of all stripes want something different. She's also glad that the race hasn't seen an influx of outside air support from national Democratic groups.    
   "I don't need them, I really don't," she said. "This is an Arkansas First campaign, and I'm an Arkansan, and I want to talk directly to Arkansans, and I want them to know that when I go to D.C., the only letters that will mean anything next to my name are the "A" and the "R."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Chris Jones, the Democratic nominee for Arkansas' 2nd Congressional District, says voters are frustrated with promises made by the Trump administration that haven't been kept.
                
                    Stephen Fowler/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Stephen Fowler/NPR
    

   
   'Folks are hurting'   On the flip side, Chris Jones has the backing of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee as one of dozens of "Red to Blue" flip targets.   At an outdoor jazz night held at a brewery in Little Rock, Jones worked the crowd between visits to polling sites and a high school football homecoming game on a campaign that has seen millions of dollars in outside spending by Republicans.   "They understand that people are in pain," he said. "Folks are hurting. They can't afford gas. They can't afford groceries. And our campaign has always been about affordability and accountability for all. So prices are way too high."   Jones also ran for governor against Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders in 2022 and lost, so he started off with higher name recognition as a serious challenger to Rep. French Hill.   He knows it's a tall task, even in a national environment more favorable to Democrats. Hill is a longtime incumbent whose district only became more conservative after the last Census-led redistricting in 2021.   But he also knows that Democrats, Republicans and independent voters alike are open to looking for something other than the current leadership.   "Here's what's so fascinating: a lot of folks here voted for the president and this administration because they wanted lower prices, they wanted to end foreign wars, and they wanted to end corruption, particularly with the Epstein files," he said. "None of that has happened, so they're super frustrated."   
   Like many states that have seen the potential for close races next week, Arkansas has a longer history of single-party control that has led to anger and frustration at the status quo and incumbency in a way that extends beyond typical partisan labels or voting history.    
   "One of the things that we forget, because there's so much that comes out of this administration: It wasn't but 15 years ago that the entire federal delegation of Arkansas was Democrat," he said. "So it's not that long ago. The reason they got in office was because of the conditions that existed, the economic anxiety and pain that people feel — and folks feeling like what they wanted to happen out of Washington was not happening. We're in that same place now."   In addition to the DCCC support, Jones has had campaign visits from former DNC Chair Jaime Harrison, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Rep. Jasmine Crockett of Texas. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear have both endorsed his run. And he's heard from people who don't normally support Democrats saying they'll back his campaign.   "Folks are literally hurting, and it's to the point where they're saying, 'my life is so bad that I don't care about party anymore'," he said.   Black voter turnout surges   Another factor working in Democrats' favor this election cycle is a surge in Black turnout following a Supreme Court decision that weakened part of the Voting Rights Act.   
   Multiple states across the South rushed to redraw House maps to gain a partisan advantage, with many of the new districts crafted in a way that minimized Black voting power. Arkansas lawmakers did not redraw their maps — the state has an entirely Republican congressional delegation — but after the 2020 Census did split Little Rock up in a manner that made Hill's district more Republican.   In primaries following the ruling, and early voting this month ahead of the midterms, there has been sustained higher Black turnout in states like South Carolina, Georgia and Louisiana in ways that could affect the outcome in key races across the region.   
   "I think part of it is that folks realized that there was an imminent threat to their right to vote," Jones said. "And people realized across the country that if we don't show up now, and Black folks realize if we don't speak up now, then our ability to do it later might not be there."   Marcus Hatley, one of the people who met with Shoffner at his family farm, said the increased turnout seemed like a "course correction."   "People are dissatisfied with the way that that happened, and some are crossing sides and voting in a different direction," he said. "And a lot of it has to do with removing, in some of those states, the ability for people of color to have equal representation in their districts. So it looks like to me there's going to be a course correction. I could be wrong, but I believe there's going to be a change."
